articles.title: Ukraine strikes deep into Russia’s Arctic gas heartland as Trump pushes Putin toward peace
articles.summary: Ukrainian drones struck Novy Urengoy, sparking a fire in Russia's top natural-gas region roughly 1,740 miles from Ukraine's border in the Arctic.
articles.body: Ukrainian drones struck deep into Russia’s Arctic north Wednesday, sparking a fire at an industrial facility in Novy Urengoy, a city in the heart of Russia’s most important natural-gas producing region, according to Russian officials and the Associated Press. Regional Gov. Dmitry Artyukhov said Russian air defenses repelled the attack but falling drone debris caused a fire at an industrial site. He did not identify the facility, and the extent of the damage was still being assessed, Reuters reported Wednesday. Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point appeared to claim involvement, posting: "Guess who covered more than 3,300 km and successfully hit the target." The extraordinary strike comes as Washington makes a renewed push to end the more than four-year war even as Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range attacks on each other. UKRAINE UNLEASHES MORE THAN 400 DRONES NEAR MOSCOW IN ONE OF WAR'S BIGGEST ATTACKS Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, President Donald Trump said he had just spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin and suggested both Moscow and Kyiv may be prepared to negotiate. "We had a great conversation. He is wanting to make a deal. And if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that would be very nice," Trump said. Asked what was holding up an agreement, Trump pointed to the personal animosity between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling them "two people that hate each other." "These are two people that are tired of fighting," Trump added. Trump’s comments followed a weekend diplomatic push by U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who traveled to Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to revive negotiations. The talks produced no breakthrough, according to the Associated Press. RUSSIAN STRIKES CONTINUE FOLLOWING VISIT BY WITKOFF AND KUSHNER TO KYIV Russia resumed major missile and drone attacks on Kyiv shortly after the American delegation left Ukraine, killing five people and wounding 35 on Tuesday, Reuters reported. A European intelligence source told Fox News Digital that the simultaneous diplomacy and military escalation reflects a longstanding dilemma for Western governments trying to engage Moscow. "You have to talk, you have to explain," the source said, arguing that communication is necessary to prevent misunderstandings. RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY But the source said Russian officials can interpret Western outreach differently. "Whenever you talk with them, they consider that this is a Western weakness," the source said, adding that the assessment was based in part on informal contacts with Russian officials. The source also said Putin’s recent emphasis on Russian "military progress in Ukraine" appeared aimed in part at Washington, projecting strength as U.S. officials seek to revive negotiations. The escalation is taking an increasing toll on civilians. The United Nations said last month that Russian attacks killed or wounded more Ukrainian civilians in July than in any month since March 2022, with 437 killed and more than 2,600 wounded. More than 16,800 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and more than 51,000 wounded since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. Moscow has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians and says its strikes are aimed at military and military-related facilities. DRONE OFFENSIVE HITS RUSSIAN OIL TANKERS AND REFINERIES AT 'INDUSTRIAL SCALE' AS MOSCOW BANS DIESEL EXPORTS United24 described Wednesday’s attack as the deepest Ukrainian drone strike inside Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Novy Urengoy lies roughly 1,740 miles — from Ukraine’s border. Artem Zhoga, Putin’s envoy to Russia’s Urals Federal District, said a Ukrainian drone had attempted to strike a fuel-and-energy facility in Yamal, according to Meduza. The city sits in Russia’s Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, the country’s dominant natural-gas producing region. About 80% of Russia’s natural gas is extracted there, according to Interfax data cited by the Associated Press. Artyukhov said there were no reported casualties. The attack was part of a broader Ukrainian drone assault on Russia. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces also struck targets around the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, including a naval base, an oil-loading terminal, military port facilities and warships capable of carrying cruise missiles, according to the Associated Press. Russian authorities said four people, including a child, were killed and 29 wounded in the Novorossiysk attack. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Russia, meanwhile, continued its own long-range campaign against Ukraine Wednesday. Russian drones struck the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, killing two civilians and wounding three, while another wave of attacks on Kyiv killed one person and wounded 14, according to Reuters. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'Not as bad as it sounds': Former attaché downplays UK-led settlement boycott impact
articles.summary: "Beyond the diplomatic steps Israel took yesterday - which I think were spot on - Israel also has economic leverage. Trade between Israel and the UK is rough...
articles.body:
Former economic attache to the UK, Shmuel Ben-Tovim, believes that Israel has economic leverage against the UK due to balanced trade relations.

Ben-Tovim highlights that the process of implementing the announced sanctions against Israeli settlements could take several months, potentially impacting the situation.

In response to UK sanctions on goods from Israeli settlements, Israel's Foreign Minister, Gideon Sa'ar, retaliated by closing the British Consulate in Jerusalem and expelling officials from the Kiryat Gat headquarters.

"Beyond the diplomatic steps Israel took yesterday - which I think were spot on - Israel also has economic leverage. Trade between Israel and the UK is roughly balanced," said Shmuel Ben-Tovim.

"From an economic standpoint, it's not as bad as it sounds," former economic attaché to the UK, Shmuel Ben-Tovim, said in a Wednesday interview with 103FM about the sanctions announced by 12 European countries against the West Bank.

"There have already been all kinds of crises in our relations. Perhaps the most prominent was in 2010 during the Mavi Marmara crisis, which caused relations to sour. After that, things eventually returned to normal," said Ben-Tovim at the beginning of the interview.

"At a rough estimate, products originating directly from settlements account for maybe tens of millions of dollars. I'd also point out that yesterday's announcement requires legislation. That process could take several months, and who knows where things will stand by then?"

Ben-Tovim went on to endorse Jerusalem's retaliatory measures, including closing the British Consulate in Jerusalem and expelling officials from the Kiryat Gat headquarters.

Israel has economic leverage against the UK

"Beyond the diplomatic steps Israel took yesterday - which I think were spot on - Israel also has economic leverage. Trade between Israel and the UK is roughly balanced."

" Britain relies on us for a wide range of goods," he added, "including in the defense sector. I think the political hit they took was immediate, whereas our economic hit will take longer to materialize. Shutting down the Jerusalem consulate is a very serious step. We'll have to see how this plays out."

Ben-Tovim's comments come after British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced an import ban on goods from "illegal" settlements in the West Bank, as well as sanctions against specific individuals and businesses providing services such as construction, instruction, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion.

Mathilda Heller contributed to this report.
